findings.source_passage: O Lord, Lord! Mum, it's quite true, and they've come over to tell his daughters. The child's safe, though, with only a bang on its shoulder as he threw it to its mammy. Poor Captain would be glad of that, mum, wouldn't he? God bless him!
findings.source_locator: carter's testimony, after 'the train came over him in no time'
findings.why_it_matters: The carter's benediction—'Poor Captain would be glad of that, mum, wouldn't he? God bless him!'—is the moral and emotional climax of the death scene, showing the Captain's goodness reflected in a working man's grief; its loss erases the chapter's central thematic statement about Captain Brown's character.
findings.suggested_fix: Restore the carter's full speech verbatim, including 'O Lord, Lord!' and the concluding 'Poor Captain would be glad of that, mum, wouldn't he? God bless him!' This is the passage's irreducible signature moment.

findings.source_passage: she came back almost calm as if she had gained a new strength. She put off her mourning dress, and came in, looking pale and gentle… She could even smile—a faint, sweet, wintry smile—as if to reassure us of her power to endure; but her look made our eyes fill suddenly with tears, more than if she had cried outright.
findings.source_locator: paragraph beginning 'Miss Pole, Miss Matty, and I, meanwhile attended to Miss Brown'
findings.why_it_matters: This is among Gaskell's most distinctive prose moments in the chapter—the 'faint, sweet, wintry smile' is a set-piece of restrained pathos; cutting it loses both the signature sentence-shape and the interpretive pivot showing Miss Jessie's fortitude.
findings.suggested_fix: Restore the full paragraph from 'Yet she came back almost calm' through 'more than if she had cried outright,' preserving 'faint, sweet, wintry smile' verbatim.

findings.source_passage: Miss Jessie told me afterwards that it, and her face too, were just what they had been formerly, when her mother's death left her the young anxious head of the family, of whom only Miss Jessie survived.
findings.source_locator: deathbed scene, after 'We hardly knew her voice, it was so devoid of the complaining tone'
findings.why_it_matters: This sentence reveals the family backstory (mother dead, other siblings dead, Miss Brown once capable and caring) and explains why Miss Brown's restored voice at death is so poignant; its absence makes the deathbed scene interpretively shallower.
findings.suggested_fix: Restore the sentence about Miss Jessie's account of Miss Brown's former self and the family history; it is brief but carries heavy interpretive weight about the tragedy of Miss Brown's wasted life.

findings.source_passage: She was evidently in a state of great friendly excitement, which she showed by eating her breakfast standing, and scolding the household all round.
findings.source_locator: paragraph beginning 'But when the morning came, Miss Jenkyns appeared at the breakfast-table'
findings.why_it_matters: This is a signature comic detail establishing Miss Jenkyns's character—tender emotion expressed as scolding and restless energy; it is exactly the kind of Gaskellian ironic aside that defines the narrator's voice in this chapter.
findings.suggested_fix: Restore the full sentence about Miss Jenkyns eating breakfast standing and scolding the household; it is brief and character-defining.

findings.source_passage: he had grown angry, and broken off entirely, and gone abroad, believing that she was a cold-hearted person whom he would do well to forget.
findings.source_locator: Major Gordon backstory paragraph, near end of segment
findings.why_it_matters: The draft reduces this to 'Angry, he had gone abroad,' losing the specific misreading—'believing that she was a cold-hearted person whom he would do well to forget'—which is the ironic crux of the whole subplot and gives the reunion its emotional charge.
findings.suggested_fix: Restore the phrasing 'believing that she was a cold-hearted person whom he would do well to forget' as it is both tonally distinctive and interpretively essential to the Gordon-Jessie arc.

findings.source_passage: When it was finished she put it on, and looked at us for approbation—admiration she despised.
findings.source_locator: paragraph about Miss Jenkyns trimming her bonnet with crape before the funeral
findings.why_it_matters: The aside 'admiration she despised' is a sharp, compressed character-portrait in the narrator's ironic register—exactly the kind of single-clause signature that defines Gaskell's voice-driven commentary on Miss Jenkyns.
findings.suggested_fix: Add back 'When it was finished she put it on, and looked at us for approbation—admiration she despised' before the hybrid-bonnet description.

findings.source_passage: Miss Jenkyns stuck an apple full of cloves, to be heated and smell pleasantly in Miss Brown's room; and as she put in each clove she uttered a Johnsonian sentence. Indeed, she never could think of the Browns without talking Johnson; and, as they were seldom absent from her thoughts just then, I heard many a rolling, three-piled sentence.
findings.source_locator: paragraph on fragments and small opportunities in Cranford
findings.why_it_matters: The draft drops 'Indeed, she never could think of the Browns without talking Johnson; and…I heard many a rolling, three-piled sentence'—a signature comic digression fusing the chapter's two central themes (Johnson/Boz rivalry and kindness to the Browns) in Gaskell's characteristic ironic mode.
findings.suggested_fix: Restore the full passage including 'she never could think of the Browns without talking Johnson' and 'many a rolling, three-piled sentence.'

summary: Three high-severity losses (the carter's benediction, Miss Jessie's 'wintry smile' paragraph, and the revelation of Miss Brown's former self at death) plus four medium-severity voice erasures require regeneration.
